cues.say: Component three: the stateless API, one service.

The API is your backend program: it takes a request, like add a pizza to my cart, and answers it. Stateless means you run several identical copies, and no copy remembers a user between requests. Carts and logins live in the database, so any copy can serve any request.
One service means it's a single program, not dozens of small ones. A managed container service runs the copies for you.
Why does stateless matter? Suppose copy one keeps your cart in its own memory.
Your next click lands on copy two. Copy two has never seen you, so your cart looks empty.
And if copy one crashes, the cart is simply gone.
The fix: no copy keeps anything between requests. Copy one gets add pizza, saves the cart to the database, and forgets it.
Your next click lands on copy three. It reads the cart back from the database, and carries on.
How does copy three know it's you? Every request carries a session token, a hard-to-guess ID in a cookie. The copy looks it up in the database.
So the copies are interchangeable. Add a fourth, and it's useful on its very first request.
What does that buy you? First, you scale out: add copies when traffic grows.
Second, a copy can crash, and no user loses anything.
Third, deploys are easy: you replace copies one at a time.
Now a real case. An hour before kickoff, the pizza shop goes from two copies to eight.
If carts live in memory, each fan is stuck on the copy holding their cart. Copies one and two overload, while six new copies sit idle.
With carts in the database, the load balancer spreads every click across all eight copies, from the first minute.
Here's where it sits: behind the load balancer. Every copy talks to the same database and cache.
So the API is the part you multiply. Anything that must be remembered lives to its right.
Two things to know. The load moves to the database: every request reads state there, so it has to keep up.
And keep it one service. Microservices, many small programs calling each other, solve big-company problems, not small-team ones.
In the interview, say: one service, run as several identical copies. Stateless, so I scale by adding copies.
